title: "Problem Authoring Guide"
toc: true

# Purpose

This library is organized as modular problem packages. Each problem owns its scenario, variables, questions, instructor answers, and images. The Instructor Builder reads those packages through a generated catalog, so professors can add problems without editing the builder code.

# Package Structure

Create one folder per problem:

```text
problems/problem-slug/
  problem.json
  variables.json
  questions.json
  index.qmd
  student-packet.qmd
  instructor-guide.qmd
  assets/
  variants/
```

The folder name should be stable, lowercase, and hyphenated, such as `pressure-vessel-tank` or `motor-driven-shaft-torsion`.

# Starting A New Problem

Use the generator:

```bash
node scripts/new-problem.mjs "Pressure Vessel Tank"
```

Or copy the package template manually:

```bash
cp -R templates/problem-package problems/new-problem-slug
```

Then edit these files:

- `problem.json`: title, summary, image, main problem statement, and engineering design goal.
- `variables.json`: instructor-editable values.
- `questions.json`: selectable student questions and instructor answers.
- `index.qmd`: library-card metadata.
- `assets/`: images owned by the problem.

After creating a package, open `problem.json` and confirm that the `slug` matches the folder name.

# Catalog Metadata

Use both concept tags and textbook chapters. Concept tags help instructors find problems by mechanics idea; textbook chapters help them align assignments with a course calendar.

In `index.qmd`, include a short controlled list of mechanics concepts plus the broader course topics and chapters:

```yaml
mechanics_concepts:
  - shear stress
  - bending
course_topics:
  - bending
  - shear
textbook_chapters:
  - Shear stress
  - Bending stress
```

`mechanics_concepts` appears directly on the Problem Library card and is searched by the library filter. Use concise, familiar terms and reuse existing wording whenever possible, such as `axial loading`, `normal stress`, `shear stress`, `bending`, `torsion`, `angle of twist`, `axial deformation`, `compatibility`, `buckling`, `fatigue`, or `factor of safety`. Prefer three to five concepts; the card displays the first five.

In `problem.json`, include the same chapter list for the Instructor Builder and generated catalog:

```json
"textbookChapters": [
  "Shear stress",
  "Bending stress"
]
```

# Images

Each problem folder should include its own images:

```text
problems/new-problem-slug/assets/problem-image.png
```

Then reference the main industry/context image in `problem.json`:

```json
"image": "assets/problem-image.png"
```

The context image appears in the library card, builder preview, student document, instructor document, and exported DOC/PDF.

If the problem has an instructor/reference idealized diagram with dimensions, labels, geometry, or the model students need for numerical analysis, store it as a problem-level image:

```json
"image": "assets/problem-image.png",
"idealizedImage": "assets/instructor-idealized-model.png",
"idealizedImageAlt": "Instructor reference idealization with dimensions and loads."
```

The `idealizedImage` appears in student packets, instructor packets, the Instructor Builder preview, and generated HTML/QMD/DOCX/PDF exports in a dedicated **Instructor Reference Idealization and Input Variables** section before the Given Data table. It is inserted after the student has completed the context reasoning and student-generated modeling work, and immediately before the numerical mechanics questions. This image is the official reference model for solving the mechanical-analysis questions.

Do not attach the instructor/reference idealized diagram to a student-generated idealization question. That question should ask students to sketch or describe their own model first. Put only truly question-specific figures in `questions.json`, such as a zoomed-in detail, alternate failure mode, or extra image needed by one question:

```json
{
  "id": "connector-detail",
  "title": "Connector Detail",
  "image": "assets/connector-detail.png",
  "imageAlt": "Close-up of connector detail for bearing stress.",
  "student": "<p>Use the connector detail to identify the bearing area.</p>",
  "instructor": "<p>Students should identify the projected contact area before calculating bearing stress.</p>"
}
```

Question images are shown in the direct student and instructor packet pages, the Instructor Builder preview, and generated HTML/QMD/DOCX/PDF exports.

# Variables

Variables are stored in `variables.json`:

```json
[
  {
    "key": "P",
    "symbol": "P",
    "label": "Applied load",
    "value": 1000,
    "unit": "N",
    "min": 0,
    "max": 10000,
    "step": 100
  }
]
```

Use short stable keys such as `P`, `L`, `theta`, `M`, `d`, or `t`. The builder automatically creates these placeholders:

```text
{{P}}
{{P_unit}}
{{P_label}}
```

Some problems also use calculated placeholders, such as a design load or computed stress in the instructor answer. List those keys in `problem.json`:

```json
"derivedPlaceholders": [
  "P_design_N",
  "max_stress_MPa"
]
```

Derived placeholders must be supported by the builder/export calculation code before they are used in questions. If a new problem needs a new calculation, add the variable inputs first, then add the derived placeholder names, then add the formula to the builder/export scripts.

# Questions

Questions are stored in `questions.json`:

```json
[
  {
    "id": "q1",
    "title": "Load Path and Free-Body Diagram",
    "section": "transition",
    "selected": true,
    "tags": ["fbd", "load path"],
    "type": "fbd/modeling",
    "difficulty": "introductory",
    "learningObjectives": ["Trace the load path", "Draw a complete FBD"],
    "gradingNotes": "<p>Look for a clear load path and correctly placed reactions.</p>",
    "commonMistakes": "<p>Common mistakes include omitting the support couple or placing reactions on the wrong body.</p>",
    "student": "<p>Draw an FBD for load <strong>P = {{P}} {{P_unit}}</strong>.</p>",
    "instructor": "<p>Representative answers should show the applied load, support reactions, and dominant load path.</p>"
  }
]
```

Each question should include:

- `id`: short and unique within the problem.
- `title`: visible in the builder and generated documents.
- `section`: one of `context`, `transition`, or `analysis`; this controls where the question appears relative to the instructor reference idealization.
- `selected`: whether it is checked by default.
- `tags`: topic labels for future filtering and review.
- `type`: question mode, such as `conceptual`, `estimation`, `fbd/modeling`, `calculation planning`, or `decision`.
- `difficulty`: question-level difficulty.
- `learningObjectives`: one or more objectives supported by the question.
- `image`: optional problem-relative image path, such as `assets/bracket-detail.png`.
- `imageAlt`: optional alt text for the question image.
- `student`: prompt shown to students.
- `instructor`: representative answer shown only in instructor output.
- `gradingNotes`: optional notes shown only in instructor output.
- `commonMistakes`: optional common mistakes shown only in instructor output.

# Editing Questions Without Writing JSON

Use the Question Editor page when you want to edit questions in a form rather than editing `questions.json` directly.

Workflow:

1. Open **Question Editor** from the site navigation.
2. Select the problem.
3. Select, edit, add, duplicate, or delete questions.
4. Check the validation messages.
5. Click **Download questions.json**.
6. Replace the problem package's existing `questions.json` with the downloaded file.
7. Run:

```bash
node scripts/build-catalog.mjs
quarto render instructor-builder.qmd
quarto render index.qmd
```

The editor validates required fields, duplicate question IDs, and unknown placeholders such as `{{diameter}}` when no variable key named `diameter` exists.

# Question Design

Every problem packet follows the same teaching sequence:

1. **Engineering Context and Main Goal**: the industry/context image, scenario, main problem statement, and engineering goal.
2. **Context and Mechanics Reasoning Questions** (`section: "context"`): function, external loads, supports, load path, critical components, likely mechanical response, and relevant parameters.
3. **Transition to a Mechanics Model** (`section: "transition"`): the student's own structural idealization or FBD, assumptions, and mechanics analysis plan.
4. **Instructor Reference Idealization and Input Variables**: the official problem-level `idealizedImage`, followed by the instructor-selected variable values.
5. **Mechanics Analysis Questions** (`section: "analysis"`): boundary conditions from the official diagram, unknown forces, equilibrium, stress/deformation/FOS calculations, comparison to criteria, and an engineering recommendation.

Student packets show the prompts in this sequence without solutions. Instructor packets use the same sequence and include the representative answer, learning objectives, grading notes, and common mistakes directly after each prompt. Keeping both packet types structurally identical makes classroom use and grading easier.

The official instructor idealization must not appear before the `transition` questions. Students should first interpret the real system and create their own model. The official diagram and numerical variables are then revealed for the common mechanics analysis.

In the Question Editor, choose the **Packet section** for every question. New questions should be assigned by purpose:

- Use `context` when the answer comes from interpreting the physical system or engineering situation.
- Use `transition` when students create or justify an idealization, FBD, assumptions, or analysis plan.
- Use `analysis` when students use the official idealized diagram and supplied values to calculate or judge mechanical behavior.

Good context-rich questions usually do not ask only for a number. They ask students to explain what the number means and whether the design is acceptable.

# Variants

Variants save common values and question selections:

```text
problems/new-problem-slug/variants/section-a.json
```

Example:

```json
{
  "id": "section-a",
  "title": "Section A baseline",
  "variables": {
    "P": 1200,
    "L": 0.8
  },
  "selectedQuestions": ["q1", "q3", "decision"]
}
```

Variants are optional. If a problem has variants, the Instructor Builder shows a Variant dropdown.

# Problem Health

Use the Problem Health page to review package completeness across the library. It reports:

- number of variables;
- number of questions;
- number of saved variants;
- missing tags, type, difficulty, learning objectives, or packet section.

The health page is generated from the same catalog as the Instructor Builder.

# Rebuild The Catalog

After editing any problem package, run:

```bash
node scripts/build-catalog.mjs
```

The script creates:

```text
data/problem-catalog.json
data/problem-catalog.js
data/problem-health.json
data/problem-health.js
```

Then render the builder and library:

```bash
quarto render instructor-builder.qmd
quarto render index.qmd
```

# Validation

The catalog script checks for common authoring errors:

- missing required fields;
- missing problem image;
- missing packet pages;
- duplicate problem IDs;
- duplicate variable keys;
- duplicate question IDs;
- unknown placeholders such as `{{load}}` when no variable key `load` exists;
- variants that reference unknown variables or questions.

Fix any reported issue, then rerun the catalog script.

# Export Assignments From The Command Line

The browser-based Instructor Builder can download Word-compatible `.doc` files and open print-to-PDF previews. For repeatable exports, use:

```bash
node scripts/render-assignment.mjs --problem jib-crane-battery-pack --variant section-a --type student --format html
```

Supported `--type` values:

```text
student
instructor
```

Supported `--format` values:

```text
html
doc
qmd
docx
pdf
```

The `docx` and `pdf` options call Quarto. If Quarto or the required PDF tools are unavailable, use `html`, `doc`, or `qmd` first.

Outputs are written under:

```text
exports/problem-slug/variant-id/
```

# Recommended Writing Pattern

For context-rich mechanics problems, structure the problem package so generated documents read in this order:

1. Main problem statement.
2. Engineering design goal.
3. Given data.
4. Selected homework questions.
5. Instructor answers, only in instructor output.

The main statement should describe the engineering role, physical system, operating context, and uncertainty. The questions should then ask students to reason, model, calculate, and make a defensible recommendation.
